question: The record of the previous run says it was terminated for exceeding its allowance. What does that settle?

options.text: That the application is leaking memory.
options.explanation: A leak grows over time. This exceeds its allowance almost immediately and does so every single time, which is a different shape entirely.

options.text: That the node ran out of memory.
options.explanation: The node is fine. A per-container allowance was exceeded, which is a local ceiling rather than a shortage.

options.text: That the application threw an error it did not handle.
options.explanation: It threw nothing at all. Being stopped from outside and failing from inside leave visibly different traces, and this is the former.

options.text: That the process was stopped from outside rather than failing, so there is nothing in the code to fix.
options.explanation: It is also why the output simply stops instead of ending in an error: a terminated process gets no chance to say anything. Reading that silence as an application bug sends the ticket to entirely the wrong team.

question: The customer argued that a configuration value could not possibly stop a process. How would you answer that?

options.text: A value that decides how much memory to reserve can stop a process just as thoroughly as any code change.
options.explanation: The intuition being applied is that configuration is inert. Some of it is a direct instruction about resource use, and that kind sits right beside the code in its consequences.

options.text: They are right, so the cause must lie elsewhere.
options.explanation: The cause lies exactly there. Accepting the premise would have closed the investigation one step before the answer.

options.text: Configuration changes are always riskier than code changes.
options.explanation: Neither is reliably riskier, and overcorrecting into that claim is no more accurate than the belief it replaces.

options.text: It depends on whether the change went through review.
options.explanation: Review affects how likely a mistake is. It has no bearing on whether this category of setting can produce this outcome.

question: The customer described it failing for about thirty seconds, recovering, then failing again. What produces that rhythm?

options.text: Traffic arriving in bursts that overwhelm the service.
options.explanation: It fails shortly after each start regardless of what traffic is arriving. Nothing about this is load driven.

options.text: It is stopped shortly after starting, brought back automatically, and then does the same thing again.
options.explanation: The interval is the startup time rather than a coincidence. A regular rhythm during an outage is usually a loop, and identifying what closes the loop is faster than treating each failure as its own event.

options.text: A health check flapping between two states.
options.explanation: A flapping check would leave the process alive throughout. Here it is genuinely terminated on every cycle.

options.text: Two instances competing for the same resource.
options.explanation: There is no contention between instances. Each one independently exceeds its own allowance.
